title: Indrani's thread
hook: a queen ties a blessed thread on the king of the gods before battle; centuries later, strangers tie them in the street
carry: anyone can tie the thread of protection
tomorrow: Janmashtami: the night Krishna was born

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shivaratri: a pillar of light with no top and no bottom. Shiva is endless. Today, the thread again, and where it came from.

Some of the stories about the protective thread aren't about a brother and a sister at all. There's a king of the gods, going out to a war he's losing, and his wife, who won't let him go empty-handed. And much later, there's a province about to be split in two, where people walk into the street and tie threads on strangers. The rakhi glittering on cardboard in shop windows each summer has a longer, stranger history than the sibling ritual alone.
screen: `NOT ALWAYS A BROTHER AND SISTER.` → `A KING OF THE GODS AT WAR.` → `A PROVINCE ABOUT TO SPLIT.`

segments.voice: First, the king. A story told in the Bhavishya Purana, and repeated at many rakhi ceremonies, says that Indra, king of the gods, was being beaten by the demons. His wife, Shachi, also called Indrani, prepared a protective thread, blessed with sacred words, and tied it on his wrist on the full moon of Shravana. He went back into battle and won. So here the thread is tied by a wife on a husband, before a fight. Second, the priests. In many parts of India, on this same full moon, a family priest ties a protective thread on the wrists of the people he serves. The thread was never only one relationship. It's a blessing you can put on anyone you want to keep safe. Third, closer to our time. In 1905, the British government divided the province of Bengal. On the day the division took effect, the poet Rabindranath Tagore called on people to tie rakhis on one another, Hindus and Muslims alike, as a sign that the people of Bengal would not be split. People walked through Calcutta tying threads on neighbors and strangers. A wife, a priest, a stranger, a sister. That's the teaching inside the thread: raksha, protection, is a sacred promise tied with a prayer, and no one relationship owns it. Anyone you'd keep safe can wear it. And that's the week. A butter thief, banana peels at Vidura's house, one Goddess in many forms, lamps for a divine guest, a boy dark as a rain cloud, a pillar with no end, and a thread.
screen: `INDRANI TIES IT ON INDRA.` · `A PRIEST TIES IT ON HIS PEOPLE.` · `1905: THREADS ON STRANGERS.` · `RAKSHA: A PROMISE OF PROTECTION.` · then, large: `ANYONE CAN TIE THE THREAD.`

segments.voice: Let a first face come, someone you'd protect, maybe the one from last time; then a second, someone who isn't family: a coworker going through something, a neighbor who lives alone, someone you disagree with. Picture tying a thread on their wrist too, and say inside: I'd look out for you. Stay with both faces for a few breaths.
Rakhi. The thread of protection, tied by a wife, a priest, a stranger, a sister. Always holding a promise.
Your line: anyone can tie the thread of protection. It was never only for brothers. That's day ninety-one.

notes: Indra and Indrani (Shachi): commonly cited from the Bhavishya Purana (Uttara Parva, Raksha Bandhan section); some tellings have the thread prepared by Brihaspati. Confirm source and details.

Tagore and 1905: the partition of Bengal took effect 16 October 1905; Tagore organized Raksha Bandhan observances that day as a sign of unity. Note: the day was chosen for the partition date rather than the Shravana full moon. Confirm the framing 'mark that Raksha Bandhan'.
Priests tying threads on patrons (e.g. in parts of north and west India): confirm and consider naming regions.
The practice extends 'name one person you'd protect' to a second, non-family person; confirm it still honors the outline.

Review (2026-10-01): the teach implied the 1905 partition day was the Shravana full-moon Raksha Bandhan ('mark that Raksha Bandhan'); it was the day the partition took effect (16 October), so the line now says that. The hook called Bengal 'a city' about to split; it was a province. Cut 'the oldest stories', 'the first rakhi', 'every August' and 'most of us know'; the fork no longer says the split was drawn 'along lines of religion'.
